title: The $1,999 Question: Can Apple Bend the Market to Its Will?
author: Daniel Nenni
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Apple’s foldable iPhone matters because it is less a test of folding screens than a test of Apple’s power to create demand for an expensive category. At $1,999, the iPhone Duo costs twice as much as premium phones, while the highest-storage model reaches $3,199. That price narrows the audience to affluent enthusiasts, loyal Apple customers and professionals who can justify a portable display.

The question is whether Apple can give folding a purpose that rivals the clarity of its products. The iPad was presented as a better way to consume media; the Apple Watch became a health and fitness device. The Duo, by contrast, is being pitched for work, entertainment, content creation and artificial intelligence. Versatility sounds attractive, but it can signal that Apple has not identified the problem the product solves.

This matters beyond one launch. Foldables remain below 3% of global smartphone sales, despite years of products from Samsung, Google and Huawei. If Apple converts its installed base, developer ecosystem and influence into sustained demand, it could legitimize the form factor, prompt better apps and accelerate investment across the industry. Even modest initial sales could rapidly give Apple a major share of the category.

But strong early demand would not necessarily prove broad appeal. Scarcity, novelty and status can carry a first generation, just as enthusiasm surrounded Apple’s Vision Pro before its price and limited everyday utility constrained adoption. The durable measure will be whether ordinary buyers see the Duo replacing both a phone and some tablet or laptop tasks.

Ultimately, the launch tests a defining Apple skill: turning advanced hardware into an obvious habit. If the company cannot explain why a foldable is worth $1,999, competitors may gain attention without gaining a mass market. If it can, Apple may reshape what consumers expect a phone to be.

Source: Reuters
